title: Why Joash Forgot the Kindness of Jehoiada’s Family
paragraphs: Why Joash Forgot the Kindness of Jehoiada’s Family
There are wounds that don’t come from enemies.
They come from people we once prayed with.
People who helped raise us.
People who protected us when we were weak.
People who carried us before we could stand on our own.
And few stories in Scripture expose the terrifying darkness of a forgetful heart more than the story of King Joash.
This is not just a story about betrayal.
It is a warning about what happens when gratitude dies.
It is a warning about what happens when spiritual covering is removed but the human heart remains unchanged.
And if we are honest… some of us are far closer to Joash than we want to admit.
The Bible says in 2 Chronicles 24 that Joash became king at only seven years old after surviving one of the bloodiest royal massacres in Judah’s history.
His grandmother Athaliah had nearly exterminated the royal line.
Children murdered.
Heirs slaughtered.
The throne drowning in blood.
But one child escaped.
Joash.
Hidden.
Protected.
Covered.
Not by soldiers.
Not by politicians.
But by a priest named Jehoiada and his wife Jehosheba.
The text says:
“Jehosheba… took Joash… and stole him from among the king’s sons that were slain.” — 2 Chronicles 22:11
The Hebrew carries the sense of rescue under extreme danger.
The phrase for “stole him” comes from the Hebrew root גָּנַב (ganab), often associated with secretly carrying away something precious before destruction can reach it.
Joash was not merely hidden.
He was rescued from annihilation.
For six years they protected him.
Fed him.
Taught him.
Raised him.
Risked their lives for him.
Imagine the pressure.
Every knock at the door could have meant death.
Every whisper could have exposed the secret.
Yet Jehoiada protected the future king when Joash had nothing to offer him in return.
That is what true covenant love looks like.
Not helping people when they are useful.
Helping them when they are helpless.
Eventually Jehoiada overthrew Athaliah, restored the throne, crowned Joash king, and helped bring national repentance back to Judah.
Under Jehoiada’s guidance, Joash repaired the Temple.
Worship was restored.
The nation experienced spiritual renewal.
Outwardly, it looked like revival.
But hidden inside Joash was a terrifying truth.
His loyalty was attached more to Jehoiada’s presence than to God Himself.
Some people look spiritual while strong mentors are nearby.
But remove the covering… and the real condition of the heart appears.
The Bible says:
“Now after the death of Jehoiada came the princes of Judah, and made obeisance to the king. Then the king hearkened unto them.” — 2 Chronicles 24:17
That one sentence changes everything.
Joash listened to corrupt voices the moment righteous accountability disappeared.
And here is the terrifying part.
The same man once rescued from destruction became the destroyer himself.
The same child once hidden in mercy became a king who murdered mercy.
Because when Jehoiada’s son Zechariah confronted the nation’s sin, Joash ordered him killed.
The son of the man who saved his life.
The family that protected him.
The people who kept him alive.
He repaid covenant loyalty with murder.
Scripture says:
“And they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the LORD.” — 2 Chronicles 24:21
Then comes one of the coldest verses in all of Scripture.
“Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him.” — 2 Chronicles 24:22
Remembered not.
In Hebrew:
לֹא־זָכַר (lo zakhar)
The word זָכַר (zakhar) means far more than mental recollection.
It means to remember with action.
To remember in a way that changes behavior.
Biblical remembrance is covenantal.
When God “remembered” Noah in Genesis, He acted.
When God “remembered” Hannah, He moved.
In Scripture, remembrance is not passive memory.
It is loyal response.
Joash did not merely forget emotionally.
He abandoned covenant gratitude.
And many people are doing the exact same thing today.
Some forget the parents who prayed over them.
Some forget the pastor who stayed up counseling them during suicidal nights.
Some forget the friend who helped carry them through addiction.
Some forget the mentor who protected them before success arrived.
Some forget the people who believed in them when nobody else did.
And once power, money, popularity, influence, relationships, or pride enters the heart… they suddenly rewrite history.
The very hands that lifted them become the hands they attack.
This story hurts because it is still happening.
Churches split because of forgotten kindness.
Families collapse because of forgotten sacrifice.
Friendships die because ego grows faster than gratitude.
People consume years of love… then betray the people who gave it.
Joash is proof that external reform without inner transformation is unstable.
You can repair the Temple externally while your heart internally drifts from God.
You can participate in worship while secretly cultivating rebellion.
You can sound righteous while remaining unconverted deep inside.
Jesus later exposed this same issue.
In Greek, Christ said:
“οὗτος ὁ λαὸς τοῖς χείλεσίν με τιμᾷ, ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτῶν πόρρω ἀπέχει ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ.” — Matthew 15:8
“This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me.”
The word καρδία (kardia) refers to the deepest center of inner life.
Not merely emotion.
The will.
The desires.
The true self.
Joash honored God publicly for a season.
But his inner heart was never fully surrendered.
And eventually pressure revealed the truth.
That is why this story is so dangerous for comfortable Christianity.
Because proximity to holy people is not the same thing as personal surrender to God.
You can sit near wisdom without becoming wise.
You can inherit spiritual environments without inheriting spiritual transformation.
You can grow up in church and still have a heart untouched by repentance.
Jehoiada could guide Joash.
But he could not choose Joash’s heart.
And eventually everybody reveals who they truly serve once accountability disappears.
The tragedy deepens even further.
As Zechariah was dying, he said:
“The LORD look upon it, and require it.” — 2 Chronicles 24:22
The Hebrew word for “require” is דָּרַשׁ (darash).
It means to seek out.
To investigate.
To demand accountability.
God does not ignore betrayal.
Especially betrayal against covenant love.
Soon after, judgment came upon Joash.
A small Syrian army defeated Judah.
His own servants later assassinated him.
The man protected from murder eventually died by murder.
Sin has a terrifying harvest.
Not because God is cruel.
But because rebellion eventually consumes everything it touches.
And maybe the hardest part of this entire story is realizing Joash once started well.
That is what unsettles many believers.
Because starting well is not the same as finishing well.
Many people passionately pursue God in one season… then slowly compromise in another.
Little by little.
Conversation by conversation.
Decision by decision.
Until eventually they become unrecognizable.
Not overnight.
Gradually.
One neglected prayer.
One tolerated sin.
One proud thought.
One ungrateful heart.
One hidden compromise at a time.
That is why Paul warned believers in Galatians 6:7:
“God is not mocked.”
In Greek:
μὴ πλανᾶσθε, Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται.
The word μυκτηρίζεται (muktērizetai) carries the image of turning up the nose in contempt.
God sees beyond appearances.
Beyond performance.
Beyond religious language.
Beyond public image.
He sees the real condition of the heart.
And this article is not merely about Joash.
It is about us.
Who are we becoming after God blesses us?
Do we still honor the people who carried us?
Do we still remember the sacrifices others made for us?
Have we become arrogant because of temporary success?
Have we forgotten the prayers that protected us when we were weaker?
Have we betrayed people who once loved us faithfully?
Some readers feel conviction right now because the Holy Spirit is exposing hidden pride.
Not to destroy you.
To rescue you before your heart hardens further.
Because the Gospel is not merely about exposing sin.
It is about redeeming sinners.
And this is where Jesus stands completely opposite from Joash.
Joash repaid love with betrayal.
Jesus repaid betrayal with mercy.
Even while being crucified, Christ prayed:
“Father, forgive them.” — Luke 23:34
The Gospel reveals the shocking mercy of God toward deeply broken people.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Yet Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet Jesus transformed him.
The thief on the cross had wasted his life.
Yet Jesus saved him in his final moments.
There is still mercy available for people who recognize their spiritual bankruptcy.
But repentance requires honesty.
Real honesty.
Not polished Christianity.
Not inspirational pretending.
Not curated holiness online.
Broken honesty before God.
Psalm 51 says:
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.”
In Hebrew:
לֵב־נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה (lev nishbar venidkeh)
A crushed and shattered heart.
God can heal a shattered heart.
But pride resists healing because pride refuses truth.
Some of you need to repent for forgetting people God used to help save your life.
Some need to apologize.
Some need to restore honor.
Some need to remember kindness again.
Some need to stop treating loyalty as disposable.
Some need to stop attacking the very people who once carried them through darkness.
And some need to realize that spiritual heritage alone cannot save you.
You need your own surrendered relationship with Jesus Christ.
Not borrowed faith.
Not inherited religion.
Not proximity to spiritual leaders.
Personal surrender.
Because eventually every person stands before God alone.
And no mentor can answer for your heart.
No pastor can repent for you.
No parent can surrender for you.
No church attendance can transform you.
Only Christ can.
And maybe that is why this story lingers so painfully.
Because somewhere deep down, many people know exactly what it feels like to either be betrayed… or to become the betrayer.
But the cross still stands.
And the blood of Jesus is still stronger than human failure.
There is still forgiveness for the proud.
Still mercy for the ungrateful.
Still restoration for the repentant.
Still healing for broken hearts.
Still hope for those willing to return.
Be honest.
This hit harder than many expected.
One day, many people will realize they did not lose relationships because others were disloyal… they lost them because gratitude quietly died inside their own heart.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Nakalimutan ni Joash ang Kabutihan ng Pamilya ni Jehoiada
May mga sugat na hindi galing sa kaaway.
Minsan nanggagaling ito sa mga taong minsan mong nakasama sa panalangin.
Mga taong tumulong bumuo sa’yo.
Mga taong nagligtas sa’yo noong wala ka pang lakas para iligtas ang sarili mo.
Mga taong nagbuhat sa’yo habang wasak ka.
At kakaunti lang ang kuwento sa Biblia na mas mabigat at mas nakakatakot kaysa sa kuwento ni Haring Joash.
Dahil hindi lang ito kuwento ng pagtataksil.
Ito ay babala kung ano ang nangyayari kapag namatay ang pasasalamat sa puso.
Babala kung ano ang nangyayari kapag nawala ang spiritual covering pero hindi talaga nabago ang puso.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… may mga tao ngayon na mas kahawig ni Joash kaysa sa gusto nilang aminin.
Sa 2 Chronicles 24, pitong taong gulang pa lang si Joash nang maging hari.
Pero bago pa siya makoronahan, halos mapatay na ang buong linya ng hari.
Pinapatay ni Athaliah ang lahat ng maaaring maging tagapagmana.
Mga bata.
Mga inosenteng anak.
Mga prinsipe.
Dugo sa loob mismo ng palasyo.
Pero may isang batang nakaligtas.
Si Joash.
Itinago.
Pinrotektahan.
Hindi ng mga sundalo.
Hindi ng gobyerno.
Kundi ng saserdoteng si Jehoiada at ng asawa niyang si Jehosheba.
Sinasabi ng Kasulatan:
“Si Jehosheba… ay kumuha kay Joash… at siya’y itinago mula sa mga anak ng hari na pinapatay.” — 2 Chronicles 22:11
Sa Hebrew, ang ideya ng “itinago” ay may kasamang panganib at lihim na pagliligtas.
Ang salitang גָּנַב (ganab) ay may larawan ng palihim na pagligtas ng isang mahalagang bagay bago ito tuluyang masira.
Hindi lang basta itinabi si Joash.
Iniligtas siya mula sa kamatayan.
Sa loob ng anim na taon, itinago siya nina Jehoiada.
Pinakain.
Inaruga.
Tinuruan.
Pinrotektahan.
Bawat katok sa pintuan puwedeng maging hatol ng kamatayan.
Bawat maling salita puwedeng magbunyag ng sikreto.
Pero hindi sila umatras.
Dahil ganyan ang tunay na covenant love.
Hindi lang tumutulong kapag may pakinabang.
Kundi nagmamahal kahit walang kapalit.
Kalaunan, pinabagsak ni Jehoiada si Athaliah at ibinalik sa trono si Joash.
Nagkaroon ng spiritual restoration sa Juda.
Naipanumbalik ang pagsamba.
Naayos ang templo.
Sa panlabas, parang revival.
Pero may nakatagong problema.
Ang katapatan ni Joash ay mukhang nakakabit kay Jehoiada… hindi talaga sa Diyos.
May mga tao kasing mukhang banal habang may malakas silang spiritual mentor.
Pero kapag nawala ang accountability… doon lumalabas ang tunay na laman ng puso.
Pagkamatay ni Jehoiada, nagbago si Joash.
Nakinig siya sa maling impluwensya.
At doon nagsimulang bumagsak ang lahat.
Ang batang minsang iniligtas mula sa pagpatay… naging mamamatay-tao.
Dahil nang sawayin siya ni Zacarias, anak ni Jehoiada, ipinapatay niya ito.
Ang anak mismo ng taong nagligtas ng buhay niya.
Ang pamilya mismong nagtago sa kanya.
Ang mga taong nagmahal sa kanya noong wala pa siyang kapangyarihan.
At sinasabi ng Biblia:
“Hindi inalala ni Haring Joash ang kabutihang ginawa sa kanya ni Jehoiada.” — 2 Chronicles 24:22
Sa Hebrew:
לֹא־זָכַר (lo zakhar)
Ang זָכַר (zakhar) ay hindi lang simpleng alaala.
Ibig sabihin nito ay pag-alalang may kasamang katapatan.
Pag-alalang may aksyon.
Sa Biblia, kapag “naalala” ng Diyos ang isang tao, kumikilos Siya.
Nang alalahanin Niya si Noe, gumalaw Siya.
Nang alalahanin Niya si Hannah, kumilos Siya.
Kaya hindi lang simpleng nakalimot si Joash.
Tinalikuran niya ang covenant gratitude.
At nangyayari pa rin ito hanggang ngayon.
May mga anak na nakakalimot sa magulang na gabi-gabing umiiyak sa panalangin para sa kanila.
May mga tao na nakakalimot sa pastor o kaibigang tumulong sa kanila noong wasak na wasak sila.
May mga taong nakakalimot sa mga kamay na bumuhat sa kanila bago dumating ang success.
At kapag dumating na ang pera, impluwensya, pride, relasyon, o fame… biglang nagbabago ang trato nila.
Yung mga taong minsang tumulong sa kanila… sila na ngayon ang sinasaktan nila.
Masakit ang kuwento ni Joash dahil nangyayari pa rin ito.
May mga pamilya na nasisira dahil namatay ang pasasalamat.
May mga ministry na nababasag dahil lumaki ang ego.
May mga pagkakaibigan na namamatay dahil nakalimutan ang sakripisyo.
Pinapakita rin ng kuwento ni Joash na posible palang maayos ang “templo” sa labas habang wasak ang puso sa loob.
Posibleng active sa ministry pero malayo sa Diyos.
Posibleng marunong magsalita tungkol sa faith pero hindi tunay na surrendered.
Ito rin ang sinabi ni Jesus:
“Ang bayang ito ay iginagalang Ako ng kanilang mga labi, ngunit ang kanilang puso ay malayo sa Akin.” — Matthew 15:8
Sa Greek:
καρδία (kardia)
Ang ibig sabihin nito ay pinakaubod ng pagkatao.
Ang tunay na laman ng puso.
Ang totoong ikaw.
At dito naging delikado si Joash.
Mukhang maayos sa panlabas.
Pero hindi tunay na surrendered ang puso.
Kaya nang mawala ang tamang impluwensya… lumabas ang tunay niyang pagkatao.
At ito ang babala para sa maraming Kristiyano ngayon.
Hindi sapat ang pagiging malapit sa mga banal na tao.
Hindi sapat ang paglaki sa church.
Hindi sapat ang Christian environment.
Kailangan ng personal na pagsisisi.
Personal na surrender kay Cristo.
Dahil darating ang araw na mawawala ang mentor.
Mawawala ang accountability.
At lalabas kung sino talaga ang sinusunod ng puso.
Bago mamatay si Zacarias, sinabi niya:
“Tingnan nawa ng Panginoon ito, at singilin.”
Sa Hebrew:
דָּרַשׁ (darash)
Ibig sabihin: hanapin, siyasatin, at papanagutin.
Hindi binabalewala ng Diyos ang pagtataksil.
Lalo na ang pagtataksil laban sa covenant love.
Kalaunan, bumagsak si Joash.
Natalo siya.
Pinagtaksilan.
At pinatay rin.
Ang taong iniligtas mula sa pagpatay… namatay rin sa pagpatay.
Nakakatakot ang bunga ng kasalanan.
Hindi dahil malupit ang Diyos.
Kundi dahil winawasak ng rebellion ang lahat ng hinahawakan nito.
At marahil ito ang pinaka-nakakakilabot sa kuwento.
Nagsimula nang maayos si Joash.
Pero hindi siya nagtapos nang maayos.
At maraming tao ang ganito.
Mabagsik magmahal sa Diyos sa simula.
Pero unti-unting lumalamig.
Unti-unting nagko-compromise.
Hanggang sa hindi na sila makilala.
Hindi overnight.
Paunti-unti.
Isang pride.
Isang lihim na kasalanan.
Isang pusong nawalan ng pasasalamat.
Isang compromise kada pagkakataon.
Pero ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo… hindi dito nagtatapos ang kuwento.
Dahil si Jesus ay kabaligtaran ni Joash.
Si Joash gumanti ng pagtataksil laban sa kabutihan.
Pero si Jesus gumanti ng awa kahit Siya ang pinagtaksilan.
Habang ipinapako Siya sa krus, sinabi Niya:
“Ama, patawarin Mo sila.” — Luke 23:34
Iyan ang biyaya.
Iyan ang Gospel.
May awa pa rin para sa mga mayabang.
May pag-asa pa rin para sa mga nakalimot.
May restoration pa rin para sa tunay na nagsisisi.
Pero kailangan ng honesty.
Hindi fake Christianity.
Hindi performance.
Hindi curated holiness.
Tunay na brokenness sa harap ng Diyos.
Sabi sa Psalm 51:
“Ang hain sa Diyos ay bagbag na espiritu.”
Sa Hebrew:
לֵב־נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה (lev nishbar venidkeh)
Wasak.
Durog.
At iyon ang pusong kayang pagalingin ng Diyos.
May mga tao ngayon na kailangan magsisi dahil nakalimutan nila ang mga taong ginamit ng Diyos para iligtas sila.
May mga taong kailangang humingi ng tawad.
May mga taong kailangang ibalik ang dangal at pasasalamat.
At may mga taong kailangang bumalik kay Cristo.
Hindi sapat ang borrowed faith.
Hindi sapat ang religion.
Kailangan mo si Jesus.
Personal.
Totoo.
Buong surrender.
Maging totoo tayo.
Mas masakit ito kaysa inaakala ng marami.
Darating ang araw na maraming tao ang mare-realize na hindi nila nawala ang ilang relasyon dahil sa pagtataksil ng iba… kundi dahil unti-unting namatay ang pasasalamat sa sarili nilang puso.
